[Decision Procedure]: extended the fragile-spot relocation list (step 3) with four more patterns drawn from measured wrong-boundary cases — reason clause '-다보니까' feeding an elliptical continuation, an adversative '-는데' clause whose adverbial modifier scopes backward over the prior clause, a '-고' clause whose conditional scope continues into a following '-면' clause, and an ambiguous entity mention followed by its disambiguating appositive — in every case the instruction is to slide the boundary to the next safe clause-final point, never to drop the split. next_changelog: [When to Segment]: added six concrete repositioning rules drawn directly from measured wrong-boundary/under-segmentation cases, each telling the model WHERE to move an already-motivated boundary rather than adding a new prohibition or removing a split: (1) chained causal explanations (왜냐면...때문에) get exactly one boundary at the outer claim/explanation edge instead of one per internal connective; (2) a '-다보니까'/'-다 보니' clause followed by a still-elliptical, verb-less continuation is not cut at the connective — the cut moves forward to where the predicate actually closes; (3) a temporal/discourse filler (이제, 그때, 그니까) sitting between a subordinate clause and the following independent main clause is cut AFTER the filler, not before it; (4) a short filler+discourse-marker cluster (e.g. 아 어 근데) may be isolated as its own segment even when it follows an already-placed boundary, as long as a substantive clause follows; (5) an ambiguous/vague entity mention is kept together with its immediately following disambiguating clause, with the boundary moved past that clarifying material; (6) a '-고' linked clause and a following '-면' conditional that jointly govern the same scope are kept together, with the boundary placed after the whole conditional rather than between them. These reposition existing latency-motivated splits to the correct clause-closure point without reducing how often the model attempts to segment.

next_changelog: [When to Segment]: added three concrete repositioning rules drawn from measured missed-gain cases: (1) an '-어서/-서' reason clause followed by an independent main clause with its own subject/verb is a safe post-clause split point (zero-cost latency left on the table in reference data); (2) a temporal/transitional filler (이제, 그때, 그니까) sitting between a subordinate clause and a following independent main clause gets the boundary placed AFTER the filler, attaching it to the preceding material, instead of leaving it fused into the main clause; (3) a short filler+discourse-marker cluster (e.g. 아 어 근데) between two independent clauses may be split off as its own brief segment even after an earlier boundary already exists, as long as a substantive clause follows. None of these remove or narrow any existing split trigger — they only add sites and reposition an ambiguous one.

[Decision Procedure]: extended the step-3 fragile-spot list with five more measured patterns, each instructing the model to SLIDE an already-motivated boundary to the correct clause-closure point rather than deleting it: (e) a '-다보니까'/'-다 보니' reason clause followed by an elliptical, verb-less continuation — move the cut forward to where the predicate actually resolves; (f) an adversative '-는데' clause immediately followed by a backward-scoping adverbial modifier — move the cut to after the whole adversative+modifier unit; (g) a '-고' linked clause immediately followed by a '-면' conditional that jointly governs the same scope — move the cut to after the entire conditional; (h) an ambiguous/vague entity mention immediately followed by its disambiguating appositive or location clause — move the cut to after the clarifying material; (i) a chained causal explanation introduced by '왜냐면...때문에' with multiple internal connectives — collapse multiple internal cuts into the single correct boundary at the outer claim/explanation edge instead of cutting at every internal connective. These reposition or consolidate existing candidate boundaries to their measured correct locations without reducing overall segmentation frequency.
